chunk_findings.detail: The `rerun` path only disables the failover chain; it does not restrict execution to the reviewer that ran the recorded chunks. Given a rerun of chunks recorded by reviewer `b` while the gate's reviewer list is `[a, b]`, line 36 sets `rest = list(revs)` and line 37 yields `a` first. If `one(a)` returns an ERROR/UNAVAILABLE result, the caller can stop the rerun on that unrelated reviewer before `b` is ever asked. This contradicts the stated behavior that a rerun asks the reviewer that ran the recorded chunks.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/failover.py:36

chunk_findings.detail: The new sentence “it is the whole try order” contradicts the new paragraph at lines 13-15. For a gate with no `gate_order`, `[review].priority_default = ["gemini"]`, and another configured reviewer `codex` with no `priority`, the doc says the critic chain `[gemini]` is the whole try order, then says `codex` “still runs as before (the resolver returns it in `rest`), separate from the ordered chain.” Thus the same configuration is documented as trying only `gemini` and as also running `codex`; an operator cannot tell whether `codex` is tried, or whether it may answer before/after the chain despite “the first that answers is the review.”
chunk_findings.title: docs/ddflow/drivers/deltas/reviewer-priority.md:5

chunk_findings.detail: The test is supposed to prove that failed reviewers are retried only after the cool-down, but it never records the fake clock at call time. A `run_chain` implementation that performs the retry pass immediately after the first pass (calling `a` and `b` again at `t=1000` while they are still cooling down) and then calls `sleep(300)` after the loop before returning would still satisfy `calls == ["a", "b", "a", "b"]`, `clock.t >= 1300`, `out.answer.status == RV.UNAVAILABLE`, and the retry-evidence assertion, even though the amendment requires the failed reviewer to be retried after the cool-down has expired. The test should capture `clock.now()` inside `call` (or otherwise assert that the second pass occurred after expiry) to make it a real regression test for cool-down-before-retry.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_review_failover.py:test_all_down_retries_after_cooldown_then_unavailable

chunk_findings.detail: `test_whole_chain_down_gate_gets_unavailable` still does not prove that the priority chain was exhausted. It only asserts that the returned pair is unavailable and that `answered_by` is empty; it never records the reviewer calls or asserts that `ev["failover"]["attempts"]` contains both `a` and `b` with their skip reasons. A `run_reviewers` implementation that treats a timeout as terminal and returns after the first unavailable reviewer would still pass: `a` returns `UNAVAILABLE("timeout")`, `b` is never called, `pairs` is `[UNAVAILABLE]`, and `answered_by` remains empty. The earlier triage said this test had been strengthened to assert both attempts, but that assertion is absent in the current file.

chunk_findings.detail: The new loop passes results produced by the failover chain to the existing `_note_degraded(... cfg.review.degraded_cooldown_s ...)` call. If a gate’s chain has one reviewer (or every reviewer in the chain fails) and that reviewer returns HTTP 403, `RP.run_chain` has already applied the failover cool-down (`failover_cooldown_s`, e.g. 300s) and returned the 403 result. The same result is then marked degraded for `degraded_cooldown_s` (e.g. 3600s). After the failover cool-down expires, the resolver would be willing to retry the reviewer, but the degraded mark still sheds it from its gate, so the amendment’s “skipped for a cool-down knob … retried after the cool-down, then returned to its place” does not happen. The documentation distinction between resolver failover and gate-pool degradation does not fix this because this code path applies both marks to the same 403 result.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/run.py:_review_gate

chunk_findings.detail: For a rerun (`prior` true), `run_reviewers` sets `rest = list(revs)` and then immediately evaluates `pairs = [(r, one(r)) for r in rest]`, so every reviewer’s `one()` call (which creates a `_ReplyFile` and invokes `RV.review`) runs before `run.py` can check `_rerun_refusal`. Given `revs=[A, B]`, a non-empty `prior`, and `A` returning an ERROR, the new code still runs `B` and creates `B`’s reply-file side effects even though the original loop would have returned `REFUSED` after `A` without running `B`. This can consume reviewer quota and leave reply-file side effects for a review that is refused without recording.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/api/review/failover.py:run_reviewers

chunk_findings.detail: The new `gate_order` and `priority_default` knob docs give incompatible chain-membership rules for a gate that has an explicit order. Given `[review] gate_order = ["critic=a"]`, `[review] priority_default = []`, and a configured critic reviewer `b` with `priority = 1`, the `priority_default` doc says `b` “joins an ordered CHAIN when it has a `priority` field,” while the `gate_order` doc says “Only the named reviewers form the chain” for that gate. The operator cannot tell whether `b` is part of the critic failover chain or runs outside it; if the implementation follows `gate_order`, the `priority_default` membership rule is wrong for ordered gates, and if it follows `priority_default`, the explicit per-gate order is not authoritative.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/config_sections/review.py:gate_order

chunk_findings.detail: The paragraph beginning “A reviewer with a `priority`...” still defines chain membership only by `priority` or `[review].priority_default`, without limiting it to the “otherwise” case introduced in the preceding bullet. Given `[review].gate_order.critic = ["lan"]` and a configured reviewer `lan` that has no `priority` and is not named in `priority_default`, lines 7–9 say `lan` “IS the chain for that gate” and “only the named reviewers form the chain,” while line 13 says a reviewer with none of these is “not part of the chain itself” and falls to `rest`. An operator following line 13 would conclude the explicit per-gate chain does not exist and the un-prioritised `lan` runs as before, contradicting the documented `gate_order` behavior required by the amendment. The doc must say this membership rule applies only when no `gate_order` entry exists, or otherwise clarify that `gate_order` names are chain members regardless of `priority`/`priority_default`.
